article-three-count.mistakeNote: Stops the count at Section 15 (habeas corpus) before the final seven provisions.
Stops the count at Section 20 (debt) and misses Sections 21 and 22.
Extends the count past Section 22, where Article III ends.

due-process-vs-equal-protection.mistakeNote: Confuses equal protection with due process when lawful steps before deprivation are asked.

due-process-vs-equal-protection.wrongChoice: The law does not require a court hearing for every application
due-process-vs-equal-protection.mistakeNote: Mistakes a due-process hearing issue for an equal-protection grouping defect.

all-four-grouping-tests.wrongChoice: The law treats all members of each group alike
all-four-grouping-tests.mistakeNote: Treats uniform rules within each group as curing an unrelated distinction between groups.

all-four-grouping-tests.wrongChoice: The law continues to apply to future applicants
all-four-grouping-tests.mistakeNote: Treats future application alone as justifying a distinction unrelated to the law's purpose.

judge-determines-probable-cause.wrongChoice: Verbal approval from a local chief officer
judge-determines-probable-cause.mistakeNote: Substitutes a local chief officer's verbal approval for a judge's probable-cause determination.

judge-determines-probable-cause.wrongChoice: The objection is incorrect because the prosecutor alone determines probable cause for the warrant
judge-determines-probable-cause.mistakeNote: Assumes a prosecutor's finding replaces the judge's independent probable-cause review.

arrest-warrant-records.wrongChoice: The objection is correct because every arrest warrant requires that personal questioning
arrest-warrant-records.mistakeNote: Transfers the search-warrant personal-examination rule to every arrest warrant.

presence-needs-no-warrant.wrongChoice: Both acts require warrants even when the officer personally witnesses the offense.
presence-needs-no-warrant.mistakeNote: Overlooks the warrantless-arrest exception when an offense is committed in the officer's presence.

search-follows-lawful-arrest.wrongChoice: The arrest is allowed, but a search of the person always needs a separate warrant.
search-follows-lawful-arrest.mistakeNote: Misses that a lawful arrest permits searching the arrested person for weapons or evidence without a separate warrant.

search-follows-lawful-arrest.wrongChoice: It permits no search of the arrested person without an additional search warrant.
search-follows-lawful-arrest.mistakeNote: Falsely requires an additional search warrant to search the arrested person after a lawful arrest.

search-limited-to-person.wrongChoice: It permits a search of any place whenever the officer first makes a lawful arrest.
search-limited-to-person.mistakeNote: Turns a limited search of the arrested person into unlimited power to search any place.

hot-pursuit-immediacy.wrongChoice: The exception applies because officers may pursue any unsolved offense without a warrant
hot-pursuit-immediacy.mistakeNote: Drops the immediacy requirement by treating any old or unsolved offense as hot pursuit.

need-not-witness-crime.wrongChoice: The exception fails only because the officer did not witness the theft
need-not-witness-crime.mistakeNote: Confuses hot pursuit with an in-presence arrest by requiring the officer to witness the crime.

need-not-witness-crime.wrongChoice: The officer must personally witness the entire offense before making the arrest.
need-not-witness-crime.mistakeNote: Confuses hot pursuit with an offense in the officer's presence instead of personally known post-crime facts.

personal-knowledge-not-tip.wrongChoice: The exception applies because any report of theft supplies personal knowledge
personal-knowledge-not-tip.mistakeNote: Treats an unverified report as supplying personal knowledge of facts for probable cause.

silence-not-consent.wrongChoice: Following an officer's order always establishes informed consent
silence-not-consent.mistakeNote: Treats obedience to an officer's order under pressure as free consent.

silence-not-consent.wrongChoice: Consent is established whenever the person does not physically resist
silence-not-consent.mistakeNote: Mistakes lack of physical resistance under pressure for clear, voluntary consent.

exclusion-any-proceeding.wrongChoice: The letters may be used because the case is not criminal
exclusion-any-proceeding.mistakeNote: Limits the exclusionary rule to criminal cases instead of any proceeding.

article-three-speech.mistakeNote: Substitutes Social Justice and Human Rights (Article XIII) for the Bill of Rights (Article III).
Selects general State Principles and Policies instead of the specific Bill of Rights guarantees.
Selects the Citizenship article instead of Article III where speech and press sit.

petition-vs-information.wrongChoice: The right to information on matters of public concern
petition-vs-information.mistakeNote: Confuses asking officials to act on a complaint with requesting access to public records.

religious-test-political-rights.mistakeNote: Confuses requiring religious membership to vote with forced labor.

abode-needs-court-order.wrongChoice: National security automatically allows officials to choose a person's residence
abode-needs-court-order.mistakeNote: Transfers national security, a travel ground, to forced relocation under liberty of abode.

abode-needs-court-order.wrongChoice: Residence and travel may be restricted under identical conditions
abode-needs-court-order.mistakeNote: Treats Section 6's distinct abode and travel rules as identical.

abode-restriction-not-absolute.wrongChoice: Liberty of abode permits no restrictions even with a lawful court order
abode-restriction-not-absolute.mistakeNote: Overstates liberty of abode as absolute even when a law and a lawful court order permit restriction.

info-check-legal-limit.wrongChoice: Deny the entire request because any claim of confidentiality is final
info-check-legal-limit.mistakeNote: Treats an office's bare claim as final without checking whether a law actually limits access.

association-lawful-purpose.wrongChoice: An association whose unlawful purpose becomes protected simply by calling itself a union
association-lawful-purpose.mistakeNote: Treats the 'union' label as overriding Section 8's requirement of a lawful purpose.

just-compensation-always.wrongChoice: No payment because the road serves the public
just-compensation-always.mistakeNote: Treats public use as an excuse to avoid paying just compensation under Section 9.

court-access-and-legal-help.wrongChoice: Permission to file satisfies the Constitution even if poverty is the sole reason for denying legal help.
court-access-and-legal-help.mistakeNote: Collapses free access to file and adequate legal assistance into one protection.

waiver-needs-writing-and-counsel.wrongChoice: The waiver is sufficient because a written signature replaces the need for counsel
waiver-needs-writing-and-counsel.mistakeNote: Treats a written signature alone as replacing counsel's required presence under Section 12(1).

bail-both-conditions.wrongChoice: The exception applies whenever the charge carries reclusion perpetua
bail-both-conditions.mistakeNote: Relies on the charged penalty alone and drops Section 13's strong-evidence requirement.

speedy-disposition-all-bodies.wrongChoice: It covers only courts hearing criminal prosecutions.
speedy-disposition-all-bodies.mistakeNote: Confuses Section 16's speedy disposition with criminal-trial rules and drops administrative bodies.

self-incrimination-forced-testimony.mistakeNote: Confuses forced incriminating testimony with security for temporary release.

servitude-needs-conviction.wrongChoice: Forced labor is described as punishment rather than voluntary work.
servitude-needs-conviction.mistakeNote: Focuses on the word 'punishment' without checking whether due conviction occurred.

debt-and-poll-tax.wrongChoice: The protection applies only if the unpaid obligation comes from a private loan.
debt-and-poll-tax.mistakeNote: Leaves out Section 20's express protection for nonpayment of a poll tax.

debt-and-poll-tax.wrongChoice: Any unpaid tax permits imprisonment because the protection concerns debt alone.
debt-and-poll-tax.mistakeNote: Overlooks that Section 20 expressly protects nonpayment of a poll tax.

complaint-not-jeopardy.wrongChoice: The rule requires a complaint but no further steps.
complaint-not-jeopardy.mistakeNote: Drops court authority, arraignment, valid plea, and protected ending from double jeopardy.

complaint-not-jeopardy.wrongChoice: Double jeopardy begins with any complaint even before arraignment and plea
complaint-not-jeopardy.mistakeNote: Assumes a complaint alone triggers double jeopardy without arraignment, plea, and a protected end.

law-and-ordinance.wrongChoice: The second prosecution is allowed because the two laws have different sources
law-and-ordinance.mistakeNote: Overlooks that Section 21 expressly bars dual prosecution of the same act under a law and an ordinance.

law-and-ordinance.wrongChoice: Only a prior conviction can bar the second prosecution
law-and-ordinance.mistakeNote: Ignores that Section 21 makes both conviction and acquittal under either law a bar under the other.

ex-post-facto-vs-attainder.wrongChoice: Bill of attainder and ex post facto law
ex-post-facto-vs-attainder.mistakeNote: Reverses the two terms between retroactive penalty increase and legislative punishment without trial.

one-law-both-bans.mistakeNote: Catches legislative punishment without trial but misses retroactive punishment of lawful acts.
Catches retroactive criminalization but misses direct punishment without a judicial trial.

public-use-still-pays.wrongChoice: A public purpose allows the government to take property without paying.
public-use-still-pays.mistakeNote: Treats public purpose as excusing payment when private property is taken.

public-use-still-pays.wrongChoice: A promise that the owner may use the finished public project
public-use-still-pays.mistakeNote: Substitutes access to the finished public project for full and fair payment.

contract-public-welfare-balance.wrongChoice: Any effect on an existing contract makes a later law unconstitutional.
contract-public-welfare-balance.mistakeNote: Assumes any impact on an existing contract automatically violates Section 10 without weighing public-welfare regulation.

welfare-label-no-erasure.wrongChoice: Calling a law a public-welfare measure permits it to erase any contract duty.
welfare-label-no-erasure.mistakeNote: Treats a bare public-welfare label as removing constitutional limits on impairing valid contract duties.

quasi-judicial-included.wrongChoice: The protection applies only if the board is renamed a court.
quasi-judicial-included.mistakeNote: Ignores that Section 11 protects access to quasi-judicial bodies based on their dispute-deciding role, not their title.

access-and-help-separate.wrongChoice: A litigant must be denied filing before a denial of legal assistance can matter.
access-and-help-separate.mistakeNote: Collapses filing access and adequate legal assistance instead of enforcing both protections independently.

legal-help-not-custody-only.wrongChoice: The Constitution protects legal assistance only during custodial investigation.
legal-help-not-custody-only.mistakeNote: Limits legal-assistance protection to Section 12 custody and misses Section 11's protection in court and agency cases.

custody-by-restraint.wrongChoice: The investigators have not yet announced a formal arrest.
custody-by-restraint.mistakeNote: Requires a formal arrest announcement instead of checking whether liberty is significantly restricted during questioning.

custody-by-restraint.wrongChoice: The suspect has not yet signed a statement.
custody-by-restraint.mistakeNote: Delays custodial safeguards until a statement is signed rather than applying them during custodial questioning.

counsel-free-if-indigent.wrongChoice: Proof that the suspect can pay the lawyer
counsel-free-if-indigent.mistakeNote: Mistakes ability to pay for a requirement when Section 12(1) requires free competent and independent counsel if indigent.

waiver-both-writing-and-counsel.wrongChoice: The waiver is sufficient because counsel heard the agreement.
waiver-both-writing-and-counsel.mistakeNote: Accepts an oral waiver in counsel's presence and drops Section 12(1)'s writing requirement.

waiver-both-writing-and-counsel.wrongChoice: The waiver is sufficient if an investigator remembers the suspect's words.
waiver-both-writing-and-counsel.mistakeNote: Substitutes an investigator's memory for the required written waiver.

secret-detention-always-barred.wrongChoice: The arrangement is allowed if questioning has not produced a confession.
secret-detention-always-barred.mistakeNote: Conditions the ban on secret detention on obtaining a confession instead of barring secret detention outright.

secret-detention-always-barred.wrongChoice: Only physical violence is prohibited during detention.
secret-detention-always-barred.mistakeNote: Narrows Section 12(2) to physical violence and ignores its express ban on secret and incommunicado detention.

admissions-excluded-too.wrongChoice: Yes, because only a full confession can be excluded.
admissions-excluded-too.mistakeNote: Limits Section 12(3) exclusion to full confessions and overlooks admissions.

section-17-before-conviction.wrongChoice: It applies only after the person has been convicted.
section-17-before-conviction.mistakeNote: Restricts Section 17 protection against compelled self-incrimination to post-conviction testimony.

bail-secures-appearance.wrongChoice: That the accused will be found innocent
bail-secures-appearance.mistakeNote: Confuses securing appearance on bail with deciding innocence at trial.

bail-secures-appearance.wrongChoice: That the case will end without a trial
bail-secures-appearance.mistakeNote: Treats pretrial bail release as ending the criminal case.

bail-exception-two-parts.wrongChoice: The official is correct because the penalty alone satisfies the exception.
bail-exception-two-parts.mistakeNote: Relies solely on reclusion perpetua and drops the strong-evidence requirement.

bail-exception-two-parts.wrongChoice: A minor charge with weak evidence merely because a prosecutor opposes release
bail-exception-two-parts.mistakeNote: Substitutes a prosecutor's opposition on a minor charge for Section 13's two-part exception.

bail-survives-suspension.wrongChoice: Suspension automatically removes the right to bail for every detained person.
bail-survives-suspension.mistakeNote: Assumes suspending the habeas corpus privilege removes the right to bail.

bail-survives-suspension.wrongChoice: The right to bail remains, but suspension permits excessive bail.
bail-survives-suspension.mistakeNote: Assumes writ suspension suspends Section 13's ban on excessive bail.

presumption-not-immunity.wrongChoice: Automatic release from every criminal proceeding
presumption-not-immunity.mistakeNote: Turns the presumption of innocence into total immunity from criminal trial proceedings.

presumption-not-immunity.wrongChoice: Automatic pardon before any court hears the case
presumption-not-immunity.mistakeNote: Confuses a starting presumption of innocence with a pardon before trial.

notice-vs-other-trial-rights.wrongChoice: The right to a public trial
notice-vs-other-trial-rights.mistakeNote: Confuses knowing the charged crime and alleged acts with keeping the trial open to observers.

notice-vs-other-trial-rights.wrongChoice: The right to meet witnesses face to face
notice-vs-other-trial-rights.mistakeNote: Confuses notice of the accusation with cross-examining adverse witnesses.

heard-by-self-and-counsel.wrongChoice: The right to have a case resolved without unreasonable delay
heard-by-self-and-counsel.mistakeNote: Confuses refusing to let the accused and counsel answer the charge with prompt case resolution.

heard-by-self-and-counsel.wrongChoice: The right to obtain defense witnesses through court orders
heard-by-self-and-counsel.mistakeNote: Confuses the right to be heard personally and by counsel with compulsory process for defense witnesses.

speedy-not-instant.wrongChoice: Treat any postponement as a violation without examining its reason
speedy-not-instant.mistakeNote: Treats every schedule postponement as a speedy-trial violation without checking the four delay factors.

speedy-not-instant.wrongChoice: Decide solely from how much time passed
speedy-not-instant.mistakeNote: Relies solely on elapsed days and omits reasons, assertion of the right, and resulting harm.

public-trial-lawful-limits.wrongChoice: Public attendance depends entirely on the prosecution's preference
public-trial-lawful-limits.mistakeNote: Substitutes prosecutorial preference for lawful grounds to limit public attendance.

public-trial-lawful-limits.wrongChoice: Only the announcement of the judgment must be open to the public
public-trial-lawful-limits.mistakeNote: Restricts the public-trial safeguard to verdict announcement instead of the trial itself.

impartiality-independent-from-speed.mistakeNote: Selects public access when the facts show judicial favoritism in an open courtroom.
Selects promptness when the defect is a judge favoring the prosecution.

confrontation-vs-compulsory.wrongChoice: The right to compel a defense witness to attend
confrontation-vs-compulsory.mistakeNote: Confuses questioning an already-testifying prosecution witness with summoning a defense witness.

absence-needs-all-three.wrongChoice: Yes, because arraignment removes the need for notice of trial
absence-needs-all-three.mistakeNote: Drops Section 14(2)'s due-notice requirement once arraignment occurs.

absence-needs-all-three.wrongChoice: No, because trial can never proceed when the accused is absent
absence-needs-all-three.mistakeNote: Overstates the rule by denying that trial in absence can ever proceed even when all three conditions hold.

absence-not-proof-of-guilt.wrongChoice: It proves the accused committed the crime
absence-not-proof-of-guilt.mistakeNote: Treats an unjustified absence after arraignment and notice as proving guilt.

absence-not-proof-of-guilt.wrongChoice: It requires the court to dismiss the charge
absence-not-proof-of-guilt.mistakeNote: Assumes an accused's unjustified absence forces dismissal instead of letting trial proceed.

habeas-protects-liberty.wrongChoice: Freedom from all state property assessments
habeas-protects-liberty.mistakeNote: Confuses detention review under habeas corpus with challenging property tax assessments.

habeas-protects-liberty.wrongChoice: Property rights in municipal land disputes
habeas-protects-liberty.mistakeNote: Confuses personal custody review with municipal land possession disputes.

both-suspension-conditions.wrongChoice: Rebellion alone makes the proposed ground sufficient
both-suspension-conditions.mistakeNote: Drops Section 15's requirement that public safety must also require suspension.

both-suspension-conditions.wrongChoice: Any emergency declaration automatically suspends the privilege
both-suspension-conditions.mistakeNote: Treats a general emergency declaration as replacing invasion or rebellion.

suspension-never-blank-power.wrongChoice: The conclusion is correct because suspension supplies a legal basis for every detention
suspension-never-blank-power.mistakeNote: Treats valid suspension of habeas corpus as making every detention lawful.

suspension-never-blank-power.wrongChoice: The conclusion is correct because public safety cancels all trial safeguards
suspension-never-blank-power.mistakeNote: Assumes suspending the writ's privilege cancels all trial rights.

covers-all-three-bodies.wrongChoice: Only a criminal trial court, with all other adjudicative bodies excluded
covers-all-three-bodies.mistakeNote: Restricts Section 16 to criminal trial courts and drops quasi-judicial and administrative bodies.

covers-all-three-bodies.wrongChoice: Only a court deciding an appeal after a criminal trial has ended
covers-all-three-bodies.mistakeNote: Limits Section 16 to criminal appeals instead of all judicial, quasi-judicial, and administrative bodies.

speedy-trial-vs-disposition.wrongChoice: Neither protection reaches the agency because it is outside the courts
speedy-trial-vs-disposition.mistakeNote: Assumes non-court agencies fall outside Section 16's speedy-disposition safeguard.

speedy-trial-vs-disposition.wrongChoice: Speedy disposition reaches the agency only after a criminal charge is filed
speedy-trial-vs-disposition.mistakeNote: Requires a criminal charge before Section 16 covers administrative agency proceedings.

coverage-not-automatic-violation.wrongChoice: The reply is wrong, so every postponed hearing automatically violates the right
coverage-not-automatic-violation.mistakeNote: Equates Section 16 coverage with an automatic violation on any postponement without checking reasons and circumstances.

applies-beyond-accused-and-police.wrongChoice: It is unavailable because the witness has not been criminally charged
applies-beyond-accused-and-police.mistakeNote: Limits Section 17 to criminally charged persons rather than any person forced to give self-incriminating testimony.

applies-beyond-accused-and-police.wrongChoice: It is unavailable because the questioning is outside police investigation
applies-beyond-accused-and-police.mistakeNote: Confuses Section 17 with Section 12 custodial investigation and restricts it to police questioning.

written-confession-is-testimonial.wrongChoice: Only spoken statements can be testimonial evidence
written-confession-is-testimonial.mistakeNote: Excludes forced written confessions from testimonial evidence under Section 17.

not-blanket-physical-ban.wrongChoice: Compulsion makes every demand for physical evidence a violation of this protection
not-blanket-physical-ban.mistakeNote: Turns Section 17 into a ban on all compelled physical evidence rather than compelled testimonial self-incrimination.

not-blanket-physical-ban.wrongChoice: It allows the witness to refuse every kind of evidence regardless of its nature
not-blanket-physical-ban.mistakeNote: Overstates Section 17 as a blanket refusal right covering non-testimonial physical evidence.

political-belief-sole-ground.wrongChoice: Any unpopular belief permits detention, while any official may impose labor without conviction.
political-belief-sole-ground.mistakeNote: Removes Section 18's safeguard against detention solely for unpopular political beliefs.

political-belief-sole-ground.wrongChoice: All detention is forbidden in every case, and all punishment after conviction is automatically unlawful.
political-belief-sole-ground.mistakeNote: Turns Section 18(1)'s bar on belief-only detention into an absolute ban on all lawful detention.

servitude-conviction-exception.wrongChoice: Any forced work is prohibited even when imposed as lawful punishment after conviction.
servitude-conviction-exception.mistakeNote: Omits Section 18(2)'s express exception for punishment after due conviction for a crime.

charge-not-conviction.wrongChoice: An accusation alone would have been enough to permit the same punishment.
charge-not-conviction.mistakeNote: Treats a mere accusation as satisfying Section 18(2)'s due-conviction requirement.

cruel-not-all-punishment.wrongChoice: Any punishment imposed after due conviction regardless of its lawful form
cruel-not-all-punishment.mistakeNote: Treats Section 19(1) as prohibiting all lawful punishment rather than excessive, cruel, degrading, or inhuman penalties.

degrading-beyond-physical-injury.wrongChoice: Only punishment that causes lasting physical injury to the prisoner
degrading-beyond-physical-injury.mistakeNote: Limits Section 19 to lasting physical injury and ignores degrading or psychological abuse and subhuman conditions.

constitution-permission-vs-ra9346.wrongChoice: The Constitution requires death for every heinous crime.
constitution-permission-vs-ra9346.mistakeNote: Turns Section 19(1)'s conditional permission for Congress into a mandatory death penalty.

constitution-permission-vs-ra9346.wrongChoice: The Constitution leaves courts free to disregard the Act's prohibition.
constitution-permission-vs-ra9346.mistakeNote: Treats Section 19(1)'s conditional wording as allowing courts to ignore Republic Act No. 9346, Section 1.

nomenclature-picks-replacement.mistakeNote: Reverses Republic Act No. 9346, Section 2 by swapping reclusion perpetua and life imprisonment.
Uses reclusion perpetua even when the violated law does not use Revised Penal Code penalty names.

no-parole-after-reduction.wrongChoice: The reduction makes parole automatic after part of the sentence is served.
no-parole-after-reduction.mistakeNote: Assumes reducing a death sentence to reclusion perpetua creates parole eligibility despite Section 3's bar.

no-parole-after-reduction.wrongChoice: The parole restriction applies only while the sentence still prescribes death.
no-parole-after-reduction.mistakeNote: Ignores that Section 3 expressly covers death sentences reduced to reclusion perpetua under the Act.

no-prisoner-penalty-choice.wrongChoice: The prisoner may choose life imprisonment to remove the parole restriction.
no-prisoner-penalty-choice.mistakeNote: Assumes a prisoner can choose the replacement penalty instead of following the violated law's naming style.

debt-and-poll-tax-both-covered.wrongChoice: The lender may obtain imprisonment by showing that the loan was in writing.
debt-and-poll-tax-both-covered.mistakeNote: Assumes putting a civil loan in writing removes Section 20's ban on imprisonment for debt.

debt-and-poll-tax-both-covered.wrongChoice: The protection applies only to unpaid poll taxes, so this loan can lead to jail.
debt-and-poll-tax-both-covered.mistakeNote: Drops debt from Section 20 and limits the protection to unpaid poll taxes.

debt-still-payable.wrongChoice: The loan is canceled as soon as the borrower cannot pay.
debt-still-payable.mistakeNote: Confuses Section 20's ban on imprisonment with canceling a valid obligation to pay.

separate-crime-still-punishable.wrongChoice: Any offense involving a financial transaction even when a separate crime is proven
separate-crime-still-punishable.mistakeNote: Turns Section 20's debt protection into immunity for separate proven financial crimes.

separate-crime-still-punishable.wrongChoice: Any conviction that requires the court to examine a written contract
separate-crime-still-punishable.mistakeNote: Treats the presence of a written contract in a criminal case as barring imprisonment.

jeopardy-vs-retroactive-laws.wrongChoice: Protection against ex post facto laws
jeopardy-vs-retroactive-laws.mistakeNote: Confuses repeated prosecution for the same offense under Section 21 with retroactive penal laws under Section 22.
Confuses repeated criminal prosecution under Section 21 with legislative punishment without trial under Section 22.

plea-required-for-jeopardy.wrongChoice: Filing the complaint alone is enough to establish double jeopardy.
plea-required-for-jeopardy.mistakeNote: Skips Rule 117, Section 7's arraignment and valid-plea requirements.

plea-required-for-jeopardy.wrongChoice: Withdrawal of a complaint is always equivalent to an acquittal after trial.
plea-required-for-jeopardy.mistakeNote: Treats pre-arraignment withdrawal of a complaint as an acquittal after trial.

acquittal-without-sentence.wrongChoice: Double jeopardy arises only after an accused has served a prison sentence.
acquittal-without-sentence.mistakeNote: Requires a served prison sentence when a valid acquittal triggers double jeopardy without jail time.

attempt-vs-frustrated.mistakeNote: Reverses attempted and frustrated stages by failing to check whether all execution acts were performed.
Overlooks that the second person completed all acts of execution before an outside cause stopped the result.

included-offense-same-elements.wrongChoice: The homicide trial may proceed because the second charge has a different name.
included-offense-same-elements.mistakeNote: Relies on charge titles instead of checking whether the first charge included every element of the second.

included-offense-same-elements.wrongChoice: The homicide trial may proceed because the second charge requires fewer elements.
included-offense-same-elements.mistakeNote: Ignores that Rule 117, Section 7 bars a later trial for a lesser offense necessarily included in the first charge.

acquittal-also-bars-included.wrongChoice: The homicide trial may proceed because only a prior conviction can bar it.
acquittal-also-bars-included.mistakeNote: Assumes only a prior conviction bars trying an included offense when a valid acquittal bars it too.

supervening-graver-offense.wrongChoice: Any conviction permanently bars prosecution for every later result of the act.
supervening-graver-offense.mistakeNote: Ignores Rule 117, Section 7(a)'s exception for a graver offense developing from supervening facts after conviction.

ordinance-and-national-same-act.wrongChoice: A national prosecution is allowed because national laws outrank local ordinances.
ordinance-and-national-same-act.mistakeNote: Assumes national rank overrides Section 21's same-act bar between a law and a local ordinance.

ordinance-and-national-same-act.wrongChoice: A second prosecution is allowed if it seeks a different penalty for the same act.
ordinance-and-national-same-act.mistakeNote: Assumes a different penalty defeats Section 21's bar on prosecuting the same act twice.

conviction-and-acquittal-both-bar.wrongChoice: Only an acquittal under the ordinance could bar the national prosecution.
conviction-and-acquittal-both-bar.mistakeNote: Limits Section 21's law-and-ordinance rule to acquittals when conviction or acquittal under either bars retrial.

requested-dismissal-reason-matters.wrongChoice: Every dismissal after a plea is an acquittal that bars another prosecution.
requested-dismissal-reason-matters.mistakeNote: Ignores that a dismissal requested by the accused for a procedural defect generally permits reprosecution.

requested-dismissal-reason-matters.wrongChoice: The request permits a new prosecution regardless of the court's reason for dismissal.
requested-dismissal-reason-matters.mistakeNote: Applies the general requested-dismissal rule blindly without checking the court's ground for dismissal.

granted-demurrer-is-acquittal.wrongChoice: Another trial is allowed because every requested dismissal waives double jeopardy.
granted-demurrer-is-acquittal.mistakeNote: Misses that granting a demurrer for insufficient evidence is an acquittal that bars retrial despite the request.

granted-demurrer-is-acquittal.wrongChoice: Another trial is allowed because only a jury can acquit an accused.
granted-demurrer-is-acquittal.mistakeNote: Invents a jury requirement instead of treating a court's granted demurrer for insufficient proof as an acquittal.

speedy-trial-exception.wrongChoice: Only a grant of a demurrer can ever protect an accused who requested dismissal.
speedy-trial-exception.mistakeNote: Leaves out dismissal for a constitutional speedy-trial violation as a second exception barring retrial.

lower-proof-still-ex-post-facto.wrongChoice: The law is allowed because it does not increase the prison penalty.
lower-proof-still-ex-post-facto.mistakeNote: Limits ex post facto laws to penalty increases and misses retroactive reductions in required proof.

lower-proof-still-ex-post-facto.wrongChoice: The law is allowed because a court will still conduct a trial.
lower-proof-still-ex-post-facto.mistakeNote: Assumes holding a judicial trial cures a retroactive lowering of the proof required to convict.

ex-post-facto-vs-attainder.mistakeNote: Confuses retroactive criminalization of an act with legislative punishment without judicial trial.
Confuses legislative punishment without a judicial trial with a backward-looking penal change.

prospective-general-crime-valid.wrongChoice: It is ex post facto because every new penal law changes criminal consequences.
prospective-general-crime-valid.mistakeNote: Calls a prospective penal law ex post facto even though it applies only to future conduct.

prospective-general-crime-valid.wrongChoice: It is a bill of attainder because Congress defined a punishable offense.
prospective-general-crime-valid.mistakeNote: Confuses defining a general offense tried in court with inflicting legislative punishment without trial.

label-is-not-proof.wrongChoice: Accept the label as proof because it names a constitutional right.
label-is-not-proof.mistakeNote: Treats an allegation or rights label as established proof without checking evidence.

label-is-not-proof.wrongChoice: Decide from the alleged harm alone without identifying who acted or what happened.
label-is-not-proof.mistakeNote: Skips checking who acted, what happened, and how the facts fit the constitutional rule.

detainees-keep-protections.wrongChoice: Reject the report because detention removes protection from punishment.
detainees-keep-protections.mistakeNote: Assumes detainees lose Section 19 protection against cruel or degrading punishment.

only-record-supported-effects.wrongChoice: A proven physical injury and difficulty meeting daily expenses
only-record-supported-effects.mistakeNote: Assumes a physical injury that has no medical or factual support in the record.

only-record-supported-effects.wrongChoice: Loss of liberty and cancellation of all the family's debts
only-record-supported-effects.mistakeNote: Invents cancellation of family debts instead of stating only the lost income and daily-expense effects in the record.

habeas-corpus-vs-parole.mistakeNote: Confuses conditional early release after partial sentence service with a habeas corpus petition testing unlawful detention.

habeas-corpus-vs-parole.wrongChoice: A request that Congress declare the relative innocent
habeas-corpus-vs-parole.mistakeNote: Asks Congress to adjudicate individual custody or innocence instead of petitioning a court.

chr-investigates-not-convicts.wrongChoice: A request that the Commission on Human Rights acquit the relative
chr-investigates-not-convicts.mistakeNote: Assigns a trial court's acquittal power to the Commission on Human Rights.

chr-investigates-not-convicts.wrongChoice: Impose a prison sentence on the officers after its investigation
chr-investigates-not-convicts.mistakeNote: Confuses CHR investigative authority under Article XIII, Section 18 with a court's criminal sentencing power.

complaint-not-conviction.wrongChoice: Treat the complaint as a criminal conviction without hearing evidence
complaint-not-conviction.mistakeNote: Treats an unexamined abuse complaint as proof of guilt and conviction.

complaint-not-conviction.wrongChoice: Replace the trial court in deciding every criminal charge against the officers
complaint-not-conviction.mistakeNote: Substitutes the CHR's investigative mandate for a trial court's authority over criminal charges.

execute-vs-decide.wrongChoice: Congress executes laws; the President settles legal disputes.
execute-vs-decide.mistakeNote: Swaps lawmaking with execution and assigns court dispute settlement to the President.

execute-vs-decide.wrongChoice: The President executes laws and alone settles actual legal disputes.
execute-vs-decide.mistakeNote: Places judicial power inside the executive branch instead of reserving dispute settlement to the courts.

veto-and-override-check.mistakeNote: Labels the President's rejection of a bill as judicial review instead of a veto.

veto-and-override-check.wrongChoice: Veto and Commission on Appointments consent
veto-and-override-check.mistakeNote: Pairs a bill veto with an appointment check instead of a congressional veto override.

senate-nationwide-and-terms.wrongChoice: 24 senators elected by district, serving six-year terms with two consecutive terms allowed
senate-nationwide-and-terms.mistakeNote: Confuses nationwide at-large Senate elections with district elections for the House.

senate-nationwide-and-terms.wrongChoice: 24 senators elected nationwide, serving six-year terms with only two terms allowed in a lifetime
senate-nationwide-and-terms.mistakeNote: Treats the two-consecutive-term limit as a permanent lifetime cap.

house-terms-not-senate.wrongChoice: Representatives serve six-year terms with two consecutive terms allowed.
house-terms-not-senate.mistakeNote: Applies Senate term length and consecutive-term rules to Members of the House.

house-terms-not-senate.wrongChoice: 24 senators elected nationwide, serving three-year terms with three consecutive terms allowed
house-terms-not-senate.mistakeNote: Applies House three-year terms and three-term limits to Senators.

house-cap-and-party-list.wrongChoice: Its membership can never exceed 250, even if a law provides otherwise.
house-cap-and-party-list.mistakeNote: Ignores the constitutional clause allowing a law to fix a different House size.

house-cap-and-party-list.wrongChoice: Party-list seats equal 20 percent of district seats alone.
house-cap-and-party-list.mistakeNote: Applies the 20 percent party-list share to district seats alone instead of total House membership.

house-origin-senate-amends.wrongChoice: The bill starts in the Senate because it concerns national revenue.
house-origin-senate-amends.mistakeNote: Starts a national revenue bill in the Senate even though Article VI, Section 24 requires House origin.

house-origin-senate-amends.wrongChoice: The bill starts in the House, and the Senate must accept it without amendments.
house-origin-senate-amends.mistakeNote: Denies the Senate's constitutional power to propose or agree to amendments on House-originated bills.

inquiry-rules-and-rights.wrongChoice: The committee may disregard witnesses' rights because its inquiry supports lawmaking.
inquiry-rules-and-rights.mistakeNote: Treats a lawmaking purpose as excusing violations of witnesses' rights during an inquiry.

no-budget-increase.wrongChoice: Congress may increase those recommended appropriations whenever each House approves by a simple majority.
no-budget-increase.mistakeNote: Allows a majority vote to bypass Article VI, Section 25(1)'s bar on increasing recommended operating appropriations.

war-vote-separate.wrongChoice: The President commands the armed forces and alone declares the existence of a state of war.
war-vote-separate.mistakeNote: Gives Congress's exclusive power to declare a state of war to the Commander-in-Chief.

war-vote-separate.wrongChoice: The President commands the armed forces; Congress declares a state of war by pooling both Houses' votes for one majority.
war-vote-separate.mistakeNote: Pools both Houses' votes into a single majority instead of requiring separate two-thirds votes in joint session.

override-separate-two-thirds.wrongChoice: The override succeeds because the two Houses together supplied more than two-thirds of their combined membership.
override-separate-two-thirds.mistakeNote: Pools House and Senate votes instead of requiring two-thirds of all Members in each House separately.

override-separate-two-thirds.wrongChoice: The override succeeds because a timely veto needs only a simple majority to reverse.
override-separate-two-thirds.mistakeNote: Uses a simple majority instead of the required two-thirds of all Members of each House.

override-exact-two-thirds.wrongChoice: The override fails because the House needs at least 225 votes.
override-exact-two-thirds.mistakeNote: Applies a three-fourths threshold (225 of 300) instead of the veto override's two-thirds threshold (200 of 300).

vp-succeeds-permanently.wrongChoice: The Senate President becomes President immediately upon the death.
vp-succeeds-permanently.mistakeNote: Skips the Vice-President in the constitutional line of succession.

vp-succeeds-permanently.wrongChoice: The Vice-President only acts as President until Congress selects a permanent President.
vp-succeeds-permanently.mistakeNote: Treats permanent presidential succession as temporary instead of serving the unexpired term.

four-year-succession-bar.wrongChoice: The successor may later be elected President because the five years were only an inherited term.
four-year-succession-bar.mistakeNote: Exempts an inherited term over four years from Article VII, Section 4's bar on later election as President.

vp-cabinet-no-confirmation.wrongChoice: Consent is required because all Cabinet appointments follow the same rule.
vp-cabinet-no-confirmation.mistakeNote: Overlooks Article VII, Section 3's express confirmation exemption for a Vice-President named to the Cabinet.

vp-cabinet-no-confirmation.wrongChoice: The Judicial and Bar Council must first recommend the Vice-President.
vp-cabinet-no-confirmation.mistakeNote: Applies the judicial nomination process to a Cabinet appointment.

sixty-day-initial-limit.mistakeNote: Shortens the 60-day initial martial-law maximum to 30 days.
Substitutes 30 days for the strict 48-hour deadline to report to Congress.

joint-majority-revocation.wrongChoice: Congress may revoke only through separate two-thirds votes in each House.
joint-majority-revocation.mistakeNote: Applies separate two-thirds voting instead of a majority of all Members voting jointly.

court-review-never-waits.wrongChoice: Only Congress may review the factual basis, and courts must wait until martial law ends.
court-review-never-waits.mistakeNote: Denies citizens immediate Supreme Court review of the factual basis under Article VII, Section 18.

pardon-after-final-judgment.wrongChoice: A pardon may remove the result of impeachment if the Senate agrees.
pardon-after-final-judgment.mistakeNote: Extends presidential pardon power to impeachment cases despite Article VII, Section 19's exclusion.

pardon-after-final-judgment.wrongChoice: A pardon may be granted before conviction by final judgment, while amnesty needs no congressional concurrence.
pardon-after-final-judgment.mistakeNote: Drops the final-conviction requirement for pardon alongside congressional concurrence for amnesty.

amnesty-needs-all-congress.wrongChoice: Amnesty requires concurrence of two-thirds of all Senators, with no House participation.
amnesty-needs-all-congress.mistakeNote: Confuses the Senate treaty rule with amnesty's requirement of a majority of all Members of Congress.

treaty-two-thirds-all-senators.wrongChoice: Yes, because 15 is more than half of the full Senate.
treaty-two-thirds-all-senators.mistakeNote: Substitutes a simple majority of all Senators for the required two-thirds concurrence.

treaty-two-thirds-all-senators.wrongChoice: Yes, because 15 exceeds two-thirds of the 18 Senators present.
treaty-two-thirds-all-senators.mistakeNote: Counts two-thirds of only the Senators present rather than two-thirds of all 24 Senators.

grave-abuse-review.wrongChoice: They may review only private disputes, never government actions.
grave-abuse-review.mistakeNote: Omits the courts' duty under Article VIII, Section 1 to examine grave abuse by government bodies.

grave-abuse-review.wrongChoice: They must accept the act whenever the body calls it a policy decision.
grave-abuse-review.mistakeNote: Treats a policy label as shielding acts beyond legal authority from judicial review.

supreme-court-15-en-banc.wrongChoice: The Court has 14 Members and hears the constitutional challenge en banc.
supreme-court-15-en-banc.mistakeNote: Counts only the 14 Associate Justices and leaves out the Chief Justice.

supreme-court-15-en-banc.wrongChoice: The Court has 15 Members and must hear the constitutional challenge in a three-member division.
supreme-court-15-en-banc.mistakeNote: Assigns a constitutional challenge to a division instead of the full Court en banc.

jbc-list-no-confirmation.wrongChoice: Both ambassadors and judges need Commission on Appointments consent.
jbc-list-no-confirmation.mistakeNote: Requires Commission on Appointments confirmation for judicial appointments.

jbc-list-no-confirmation.wrongChoice: The Judicial and Bar Council appoints judges directly from its own list.
jbc-list-no-confirmation.mistakeNote: Confuses the Council's nominating role with the President's appointment power.

district-one-year-residence.wrongChoice: She meets the district residence rule because voter registration replaces it.
district-one-year-residence.mistakeNote: Treats district voter registration as substituting for one full year of district residence.

district-one-year-residence.wrongChoice: She meets the district residence rule because only six months are required.
district-one-year-residence.mistakeNote: Confuses the six-month local voting residence rule with the one-year requirement for district Representatives.

age-measured-election-day.wrongChoice: She fails the age requirement because she must already be 40 when filing her candidacy.
age-measured-election-day.mistakeNote: Measures the minimum age at candidacy filing instead of on election day.

age-measured-election-day.wrongChoice: She fails the age rule because district representatives must be at least 35.
age-measured-election-day.mistakeNote: Applies the Senate's 35-year minimum age to a district Representative.

vp-ten-year-residence.wrongChoice: She meets the residence requirement because the Vice-President needs only two years.
vp-ten-year-residence.mistakeNote: Applies the Senate's two-year residence rule to the Vice-Presidency.

vp-ten-year-residence.wrongChoice: She meets the residence requirement because it applies only to presidential candidates.
vp-ten-year-residence.mistakeNote: Overlooks that Article VII, Section 3 gives the Vice-President the same ten-year residence rule as the President.

supreme-court-all-three.wrongChoice: A natural-born citizen, age 39, with 16 years of Philippine law practice
supreme-court-all-three.mistakeNote: Allows extra years of law practice to excuse failing the 40-year minimum age.

supreme-court-all-three.wrongChoice: A naturalized citizen, age 45, with 20 years of Philippine law practice
supreme-court-all-three.mistakeNote: Allows naturalized citizenship with long experience despite the natural-born requirement.

lower-collegiate-natural-born.wrongChoice: Every lower-court judge must satisfy the Supreme Court’s age and experience minimums.
lower-collegiate-natural-born.mistakeNote: Applies Supreme Court age and 15-year experience thresholds to every lower court.

lower-collegiate-natural-born.wrongChoice: Congress cannot set further qualifications once citizenship and Bar membership are met.
lower-collegiate-natural-born.mistakeNote: Ignores Article VIII, Section 7(2), which directs Congress to set lower-court qualifications.

qualities-beyond-bar.wrongChoice: Lower-court judges need no proven integrity if they are Philippine Bar members.
qualities-beyond-bar.mistakeNote: Treats Philippine Bar membership as waiving Article VIII, Section 7(3)'s integrity requirement.

comelec-chair-in-majority.wrongChoice: Every COMELEC member must have ten years of law practice.
comelec-chair-in-majority.mistakeNote: Applies the ten-year lawyer requirement to all seven COMELEC members instead of a majority including the Chair.

comelec-chair-in-majority.wrongChoice: Four qualified lawyers cannot form a majority of seven members.
comelec-chair-in-majority.mistakeNote: Miscounts four out of seven as not a majority while missing that the Chair must be in that majority.

coa-no-same-profession.wrongChoice: A CPA with twelve years of auditing experience who is not a lawyer
coa-no-same-profession.mistakeNote: Picks a third CPA when two seats are already CPAs, violating the mixed-profession rule.

coa-no-same-profession.wrongChoice: A lawyer with nine years of law practice who is not a CPA
coa-no-same-profession.mistakeNote: Accepts nine years of practice even though Article IX-D, Section 1(1) requires at least ten years.

ombudsman-prior-candidacy.wrongChoice: She may be appointed because only losing candidates are barred from this office.
ombudsman-prior-candidacy.mistakeNote: Narrows Article XI, Section 8's prior-candidacy bar to losing candidates only.

ombudsman-prior-candidacy.wrongChoice: She may be appointed because legal experience cancels the candidacy restriction.
ombudsman-prior-candidacy.mistakeNote: Treats meeting the legal-experience rule as waiving the separate bar on prior candidacy.
